# Crossing Over: Some Thoughts on the Subscription Transition

Before anything else, one observation worth sitting with: the competitor didn't lose a fifth of their customers to subscriptions. They lost them to abruptness. The trough we're modeling is a financial problem, and financial problems have shapes you can manage. Trust, once spent, doesn't come back on any schedule. So I'd be tempted to treat the installed base's sense of entitlement not as an obstacle but as the asset it actually is — loyalty wearing a disguise — and design everything else around that reading.

## What do we owe the people who already paid?

The instinct in these transitions is to design the new offer. I'd start by designing what *doesn't* change. Say early, loudly, and in writing: every license ever sold keeps working. No forced migration, no end-of-support ambush. This costs us little and buys the one thing the competitor never had — patience from the base.

Then make the subscription the obviously better path rather than the only path:

- **Let perpetual fall behind gently.** New capabilities, integrations, and performance work land in the subscription first, then exclusively. No announcement needed. Customers read product velocity better than any pricing page.
- **Treat the sunk license as a prepaid annuity.** Credit a meaningful portion of what they originally paid across their first two or three subscription years. The psychology matters more than the math: we're honoring their purchase, not asking them to pretend it never happened.
- **Meet them at the upgrade moment.** Every paid-upgrade decision is a natural crossroads. Price the subscription against the *upgrade price*, not against zero, and the comparison does our work for us.
- **The unconventional piece I'd push for:** a perpetual fallback. After, say, three years of continuous subscription, a customer who leaves keeps the then-current version forever. This quietly dissolves the ownership objection — subscription becomes a path to eventual ownership rather than its surrender. It also keeps us honest about delivering enough value that nobody wants to leave.

And for the fifth who'd otherwise churn — they're not one group. Occasional users get a lighter tier. The philosophically attached get paid extended maintenance: a shrinking, profitable, dignified tail. Nobody is cornered.

## Pricing the crossing

The interesting question isn't "what's the subscription price" — it's "what conversion curve do we want," since the trough's depth is set by the mix, not the sticker.

A sketch worth testing: year one priced near the maintenance renewal customers already pay without flinching; three-year TCO landing roughly where license-plus-maintenance-plus-one-upgrade would have put them; a three-year price lock for anyone who migrates in the first twelve months, with a published escalator after. The lock creates urgency without force — an invitation with a deadline, not an ultimatum.

Model it honestly and the picture is usually this: deep enough incentive to pull 60–70% of the base across in 24–30 months, priced high enough that year-three ARR clears the old revenue peak. If both can't be true at once, the offer's value is the problem, not the price.

## What happens to a rep's W-2?

Nobody in sales asks whether the transition is good for the company. They ask what it does to their income, and they'll answer it themselves if we don't answer first.

Comp neutrality at the start — a subscription deal pays what the equivalent perpetual would have — then a deliberate tilt. Accelerators for multi-year prepay (which also repairs the cash trough, which runs deeper than the revenue trough). A specific bounty for migrating installed-base accounts, since that's the work that actually matters. A modest kicker on ARR still retained at twelve months, so signatures come with adoption attached. Clawbacks on early churn keep everyone honest.

One thing I'd guard jealously: bridge guarantees and quota relief through the trough. Losing revenue is survivable. Losing the best reps mid-valley, right when the base needs shepherding, is the catastrophe that doesn't show up in the model.

## Telling the story before the numbers do

Investors forgive a forecast valley. They don't forgive a surprise one. So we name the trough ourselves, draw its shape, and hand out a new scoreboard before the old one turns ugly: ARR, net revenue retention, recurring percentage, deferred revenue, cash. Report recurring and non-recurring lines separately so the growing annuity stays visible inside the shrinking total — the dip and the build at the same time, in plain sight.

For the board, milestones rather than faith: installed-base conversion rate, an NRR floor, a cash floor, with explicit tripwires for what we'd reconsider. A monitored descent is an easier commitment than a leap. Management comp tied to ARR metrics tells both audiences we're eating the same meal we're serving. And the Adobe and Autodesk maps are worth leaving on the table — the other side of this valley is well documented.

Two quiet moves I'd tuck in: an investor day with the full model *before* the first soft quarter, and a final, well-marketed perpetual release sold right up to the starting gun. There's a pleasing symmetry in the old model funding its own succession.

## The part I'd resist

The temptation will be a program office, a steering committee, a hundred-row plan. I'd push back on that. A small team with real expertise, direct access to the numbers, and freedom to adjust pricing and incentives as the conversion data comes in will outrun any governance structure. Rigidity is what killed the competitor's base; let's not install it internally.

And before the big announcement — a quiet pilot. Twenty friendly accounts, the migration offer, ninety days of listening. Whatever survives contact with them is the real plan.

Which twenty customers would you call first? That answer probably tells us more than the model does.
